records.p: The long curved bill and patterned head distinguish this coastal wader (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). A striped crown with dark central band accompanies a long downcurved bill (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Eurasian Whimbrel has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Davao del Norte, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026; Gamalo et al., 2023). Eurasian Whimbrels probe sand and mud with a curved bill, taking crabs and other intertidal invertebrates (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, n.d.). The Eurasian Whimbrel is associated with coastal and intertidal habitats.

r.short: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, n.d.

records.p: Nonbreeding birds are grey above and white below with an extremely fine black bill and dark facial patch; breeding females have red neck patches (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-necked Phalarope has been documented on Mindanao and Samar. On Mindanao, records include Panabo–Carmen wetlands and Davao del Norte. On Samar, records include Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-necked Phalarope frequently swims while spinning to bring small aquatic invertebrates to the surface; nonbreeding birds are often pelagic (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The historical account describes patterned, down-covered chicks, with tawny upperparts and dark stripes across the rump (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Red-necked Phalarope is associated with freshwater wetlands, coastal and intertidal habitats, and offshore waters.

The Bukidnon Woodcock has a dark, finely mottled back marked by two parallel pale scapular lines and cinnamon-rufous notches in the wing feathers. Its cinnamon throat and breast bear broad dark barring, which continues onto the paler belly and undertail-coverts. Kennedy and colleagues compared these markings with other Asian woodcocks when describing the species (Kennedy et al., 2001). The Bukidnon Woodcock has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Balatukan, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Tagubud, and Misamis Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Bukidnon Woodcock inhabits tropical moist forest, including montane forest, rather than the open coastal mudflats used by many other shorebirds (BirdLife International, 2024). AVONET lists a culmen length of 85.9 mm, wing length of 161 mm, tail length of 58 mm, and body mass of 238 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 7 mm, bill depth of 11.1 mm, and tarsus length of 33.7 mm for Scolopax bukidnonensis (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 69.1 mm, Kipp’s distance of 32.2 mm and wing length of 161 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 20.0 (Tobias et al., 2022).

Short yellow legs, a blunt-tipped bill and chevron-marked breeding underparts distinguish it (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Grey-tailed Tattler is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Agusan del Sur and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Feeds on rocky shorelines and tidal pools, taking invertebrate prey (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Historical observers recorded migrating birds feeding on tidal flats, sometimes in considerable numbers (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Breeding plumage is predominantly black, with pale upperpart spotting (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Spotted Redshank has been reported from Mindanao, where the Philippine Red List documents a rare occurrence (Philippine Red List Committee, 2020). The Spotted Redshank is broadly associated with coastal and intertidal habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

Spotted upperparts, long pale legs and a strong supercilium distinguish this sandpiper (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Wood Sandpiper has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Sur, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Wood Sandpiper feeds by probing small freshwater pools and muddy margins (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). McGregor described abrasion of pale feather edges during the breeding season, changing the appearance of upperpart spotting (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Wood Sandpiper is associated with freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Relative to Common Greenshank, it has thicker neck and bill but shorter legs (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Nordmann's Greenshank is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Spotted Greenshank uses estuaries, coastal mudflats and lowland swamps outside the breeding season, occasionally visiting wet meadows, saltpans and rice fields. Its northern breeding habitats differ from these tropical wetland settings (BirdLife International, 2024). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

Its long greenish legs and upturned bill distinguish it from Marsh Sandpiper (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Greenshank has been documented on Mindanao, including Zamboanga del Sur, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Common Greenshank hunts small fish and other animals in shallow coastal water with rapid bill strikes (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Greenshank is associated with freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Compared with Common Sandpiper, it has longer legs, a more continuous dark breast band and a much clearer white rump in flight (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Green Sandpiper is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Green Sandpiper often feeds alone or in small groups at freshwater edges, sometimes alongside Wood Sandpiper (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). McGregor described seasonal replacement of worn winter plumage through a molt occurring while birds remained in wintering areas (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Green Sandpiper is associated with forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams.

A fine straight bill and unusually long thin legs distinguish it from the heavier, up-billed Common Greenshank (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Marsh Sandpiper has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Sur, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Marsh Sandpiper wades through shallow water and pecks prey from the surface, often alongside other shorebirds (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Marsh Sandpiper is associated with freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines.

Orange-red legs and a white wing trailing-edge separate it from Spotted Redshank (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Redshank has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Zamboanga del Sur, Davao del Norte, and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Forages by walking and probing in tidal pools and shallow estuarine mud (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A markedly upturned bill and short orange legs distinguish this shorebird (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Terek Sandpiper has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026). The Terek Sandpiper runs actively along intertidal edges, searching soft mud and shoreline debris for prey (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Terek Sandpiper is associated with coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Pomarine Jaeger is a substantial, broad-bodied jaeger with a relatively heavy bill and rounded head profile. Breeding adults can have broad, rounded projections of the central tail feathers and a dark spotted band across the breast. Young birds are more difficult to separate, often showing a strongly barred undertail and two pale zones on the underwing (Carey and Pang, 2024). The Pomarine Jaeger is recorded on Mindanao (Avibase, 2026). The Pomarine Jaeger is associated with coastal and intertidal habitats as well as offshore waters. At sea, Pomarine Jaegers may seize food from other birds, catch small prey at the water surface or hunt birds in flight (National Audubon Society, n.d.). AVONET lists a culmen length of 45.8 mm, wing length of 350.8 mm, tail length of 175.6 mm, and body mass of 692.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 7.2 mm, bill depth of 12.5 mm, and tarsus length of 52 mm for Stercorarius pomarinus (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 16.1 mm, Kipp’s distance of 196.1 mm and wing length of 350.8 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 55.9 (Tobias et al., 2022).

The Small Buttonquail has finely mottled brown, black and grey upperparts with buff lines along the crown and sides of the back. Females are generally larger and more strongly colored, with a chestnut breast, white upper throat and pale belly. Males are duller. Plumage and measurements vary geographically, so these characters should be used together (Pappas, 2002). The Common Buttonquail has records from Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Common Buttonquail is broadly associated with grasslands, other open habitats, shrubland and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14 mm, wing length of 83.8 mm, tail length of 42 mm, and body mass of 52.7 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 2.2 mm, bill depth of 3.8 mm, and tarsus length of 21.9 mm for Turnix sylvaticus (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 7.3 mm, Kipp’s distance of 23 mm and wing length of 83.8 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 27.4 (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: The Asian Woollyneck is a large, mostly glossy-black stork with an elongated, almost woolly white neck and contrasting white lower belly and tail. Adults have a sharply defined black crown, bare bluish-grey facial skin, a long dark bill with a reddish tip and orange-red legs (BirdLife International, 2020). The Asian Woolly-necked Stork is recorded on Mindanao (GBIF.org, 2026). The Asian Woolly-necked Stork is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers, streams and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 149.4 mm, wing length of 456.2 mm, tail length of 169.3 mm, and body mass of 2061 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 18.1 mm, bill depth of 27.3 mm, and tarsus length of 155.3 mm for Ciconia episcopus (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET comparative measurements give a beak length (tip to nares) of 123.8 mm, Kipp’s distance of 174 mm and wing length of 456.2 mm. The hand-wing index calculated from these averages is approximately 38.1 (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

Long metallic green neck hackles, a white tail, and dark bronze-green plumage distinguish adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Nicobar Pigeon has been documented on Leyte, including Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GIZ, 2013). The Nicobar Pigeon inhabits wooded coastal islands and often forages on the ground. It may move between offshore islands (Sarawak Forest Department, n.d.). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

records.p: Metallic green-bronze wings, a pale forehead, and pinkish breast identify adult males (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Common Emerald Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Common Emerald Dove spends much of its time on the ground in woodland and often returns to the forest floor after being disturbed (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Wild-type birds are grey with two black wing bars and iridescent green-purple neck feathers; feral plumages vary widely (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Rock Dove is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, and Davao del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Rock Dove is associated with agricultural areas as well as settlements and disturbed habitats. Feral populations occupy urban environments throughout their introduced range (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Metallic Wood Pigeon is a large, dark, glossy pigeon with a white throat. Its dark slaty nape, back and wings have metallic green reflections, while the forehead and lower body are purplish-grey with a lilac sheen. The bare skin around the eye is crimson, and the bill is yellow with a reddish base (Forest Department Sarawak, n.d.). The Metallic Pigeon has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Metallic Pigeon is broadly associated with forests and cultivated land. AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 14 mm, Kipp’s distance of 70.3 mm, and wing length of 216.4 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 32.5 (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.full: Forest Department Sarawak. (n.d.). Metallic Wood Pigeon (Columba vitiensis). https://forestry.sarawak.gov.my/web/subpage/webpage_view/907

records.p: A broad-bodied green imperial pigeon with a metallic sheen on upperparts and maroon-chestnut undertail coverts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Green Imperial Pigeon has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Apo Natural Park on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Green Imperial Pigeons feed extensively on canopy fruit, often moving among fruiting trees alone or in small groups (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The pale cream-white body contrasts sharply with black flight feathers and a broad dark terminal tail band (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Pied Imperial Pigeon has been documented on Mindanao and Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026). Pied Imperial Pigeons feed on fruit including figs and palm fruits and may gather in flocks near fruiting trees (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Pied Imperial Pigeon is associated with forests and agricultural land, as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Spotted Imperial Pigeon has greyish head and forebody coloration, with fine paler flecking or spotting across portions of the upperparts. The adult male is described with a pale crescent across the upper breast and a darker band below, while females are darker and show a less contrasting chest. Such differences require attention to sex and subspecies rather than reliance on one plumage mark (BirdForum Opus, n.d.). The Spotted Imperial Pigeon has been documented on Mindanao and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Tagubud, Lake Lanao, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). Historical naturalists observed birds feeding on large seeds and nuts, sometimes congregating in fruiting trees (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Spotted Imperial Pigeon is associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 25.1 mm, wing length of 209.2 mm, tail length of 120.2 mm, and body mass of 289 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 6 mm, bill depth of 5.6 mm, and tarsus length of 25.9 mm for Ducula carola (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 12.9 mm, Kipp’s distance of 76 mm, and wing length of 209.2 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 36.3 (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

The Pink-bellied Imperial Pigeon has a whitish-grey forehead and purplish-grey crown, bronze to emerald-green back and wings, and a green breast contrasting with a pale pinkish-grey abdomen. The tail has a broad white transverse band, and the bare orbital skin and feet are bright red (DENR WildALERT, n.d.). The Pink-bellied Imperial Pigeon has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Pink-bellied Imperial Pigeon is broadly associated with forests. AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 13.5 mm, Kipp’s distance of 63.4 mm, and wing length of 212 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 29.9 (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

The Mindanao Bleeding-heart has a metallic green head and upperparts, a contrasting white throat and a conspicuous red patch centered on the breast. These characters are illustrated in the University of California, Irvine, museum-photo account, which records no obvious sex-related plumage difference in its photographed birds (Avise, n.d.). The Mindanao Bleeding-heart is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Leyte, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Mindanao Bleeding-heart is described as a mainly ground-dwelling dove of primary and secondary lowland dipterocarp forest (Wild Bird Club of the Philippines, 2025). AVONET reports average beak length (tip to nares) of 10.3 mm, Kipp’s distance of 43 mm, and wing length of 150.2 mm. The corresponding hand-wing index is approximately 28.6 (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

records.p: Fine dark barring across the neck and flanks contrasts with a pinkish breast and gray face (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Zebra Dove has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Zebra Dove is associated with grasslands and other open areas as well as agricultural areas. The nest is a flimsy platform of twigs, generally holding two white eggs (McGregor, 1909–1910).

A long graduated tail, rich chestnut underparts, and iridescence on the sides of the neck characterize this cuckoo-dove (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Cuckoo-Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Cuckoo-Dove is broadly associated with forests.

Brown plumage carries an amethyst iridescence on the neck, with pale and dark facial stripes and a gray terminal tail band (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Amethyst Brown Dove has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Mount Capotoan on Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Amethyst Brown Dove is associated with forests. The Hijo inventory describes a deep, hoop-like call and a low growling vocalization. The species was photographed during birding in 2019 but detected only by voice in the later survey (Gamalo et al., 2023). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: The dark brown crown, amethystine hindneck patch, pearly gray breast and ochraceous-brown lower body distinguish this pigeon (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Mindanao Brown Dove has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Tagubud, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The regional checklist associates the Mindanao Brown Dove with forest habitats and coastal and intertidal environments. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

This small brown dove has a pale stripe below and behind the eye bordered by darker facial plumage, with bronze-green to purple iridescence across the hindneck and upper back. The tail is brown with a grey tip, and the legs are pinkish to red (WildAlert, n.d.). The White-eared Brown Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, Siargao, and Basilan, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The White-eared Brown Dove is broadly associated with forests. Nests recorded on Mindoro were made of twisted tendrils, supported on horizontal branches about 2–6 m above ground (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Adult males have a black chin, pearl-gray head, throat and breast, green wings and a dark chestnut band below the breast; females are greener on the throat and breast (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-chinned Fruit Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Black-chinned Fruit Dove feeds among fruiting forest trees and is seldom observed on the ground (McGregor, 1909–1910).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 17.7 mm, wing length of 118.1 mm, tail length of 75.1 mm, and body mass of 92 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 3.9 mm, bill depth of 4.3 mm, and tarsus length of 21 mm for Ptilinopus melanospilus (Tobias et al., 2022). The Black-naped Fruit Dove has been documented on Mindanao and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Pasonanca area (GBIF.org, 2026). The regional checklist associates the Black-naped Fruit Dove with forest habitats, shrubland, settlements and disturbed land, and coastal and intertidal environments.

A crimson-to-purple hindcrown and conspicuous yellow breast patch interrupt an otherwise green body (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Yellow-breasted Fruit Dove is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Yellow-breasted Fruit Dove is broadly associated with forests.

The spotted black-and-white neck patch contrasts with a warm pink-brown body and long white-tipped tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Spotted Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Spotted Dove is associated with forests edges, shrublands, and agricultural areas. The Spotted Dove feeds mostly on grains and seeds on the ground, commonly in pairs or small groups (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A slender brown-pink dove with a narrow black half-collar and pale edging at the tail corners (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Collared Dove has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Agusan del Sur, and Davao Oriental. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Collared Dove is broadly associated with grasslands and other open habitats, shrubland, cultivated land, and settlements and disturbed habitats. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Endangered (EN).

Males have a grey head, wine-red body, black hindneck collar and contrasting slate-coloured lower back; females are dull sandy brown (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red Collared Dove has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Melibengoy, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Red Collared Dove is associated with grasslands and other open areas as well as agricultural areas. The Red Collared Dove feeds mainly on seeds on the ground, generally in pairs or small groups (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The adult male carries a contrasting maroon shoulder and upper back against a predominantly green body (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Green Pigeon is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur. On Samar, records include Northern Samar. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The regional checklist associates the Philippine Green Pigeon with forest habitats and caves and karst landscapes. Historical observers described fruit-tree feeding, sometimes in mixed gatherings with Pink-necked Green Pigeons (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Male plumage includes a gray head, pinkish nape, orange breast, and green belly (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Pink-necked Green Pigeon is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Bega Watershed. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). Forages in fruiting trees, often in groups, and seldom visits the ground except to drink (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). A historical account describes a loose platform nest made of twigs, grasses and tendrils, about 18 cm wide, with a white egg (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The 2024 global assessment describes a Mindanao endemic of montane forests (~1,000–2,400 m range) with a blue head, orange-red bill and distinctive voice. The Blue-capped Kingfisher has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Malindang Range, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Pasian, and Agusan del Norte (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Blue-capped Kingfisher inhabits montane forest on Mindanao, with occasional records from secondary or disturbed forest. It is often inconspicuous but vocalizes before dawn (BirdLife International, 2024). The 2024 IUCN range account places the Blue-capped Kingfisher on Mindanao where suitable forest persists, including more localities than older records suggested (BirdLife International, 2024). The same assessment describes a suspected decline (BirdLife International, 2024). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

A small kingfisher with bright turquoise upperparts, orange underparts and a white throat; females have reddish colour on the lower bill (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Kingfisher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Pasonanca area. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Common Kingfisher is associated with freshwater wetlands as well as riverbanks and shorelines. The Common Kingfisher takes small fish by diving from a perch, then strikes prey against the perch (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Southern Silvery Kingfisher has a black crown and wings, small white spots running back along the crown, and a contrasting white patch behind each ear. Its back and rump are silvery-white, the throat and upper breast are white, and the dark lower breast and flanks have a blue wash. The bill is black and the feet red (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Southern Silvery Kingfisher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Southern Silvery Kingfisher is broadly associated with forests and habitats along rivers and streams. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Compared with the southern Silvery Kingfisher, the Northern Silvery Kingfisher shows a deeper ultramarine to purplish-blue wash over the otherwise black breast and sides. Its dark bill and bright scarlet feet were recorded for both sexes; buff on the throat and abdomen of some specimens was considered possibly age-related (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Northern Silvery Kingfisher is recorded on Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park and Mount Capotoan (GBIF.org, 2026). The Northern Silvery Kingfisher is broadly associated with forests, rivers and streams. Small crabs were identified in one historical dietary observation; a specimen account recorded bright-red feet (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

A very small kingfisher with a large red bill, blue upperparts and orange underparts, occurring in darker and paler plumage forms. The lores and moustachial area are orange rather than the blue or black shown by several similar dwarf kingfishers; a white throat grades into the orange upper breast (BirdLife International, 2016). The Dimorphic Dwarf Kingfisher has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan del Sur, Davao Oriental, and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The Dimorphic Dwarf Kingfisher is broadly associated with forests and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 35.6 mm, wing length of 62.9 mm, tail length of 22.9 mm, and body mass of 21.3 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 6 mm, bill depth of 7.7 mm, and tarsus length of 13.8 mm for Ceyx margarethae (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Other Threatened Species (OTS).

records.p: In the contemporary North Philippine Dwarf-kingfisher concept, this is a tiny rufous bird with a lilac wash over parts of the crown, ear-coverts and breast, a white throat and belly, and a blue-and-white patch on the side of the neck. The back carries a dark V-shaped mark; the bill and legs are bright red (BirdLife International, 2024). The Philippine Dwarf Kingfisher has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Philippine Dwarf Kingfisher is broadly associated with forests and habitats along rivers and streams. Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Adults are richly rufous with a bright red bill and bluish pale rump; juveniles are browner with dark bars below (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Ruddy Kingfisher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, and Leyte, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Ruddy Kingfisher is associated with forests. The Ruddy Kingfisher feeds on fishes, crustaceans and larger insects, also taking amphibians (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Rufous head and breast, blue upperparts, a white throat, and a strong reddish bill characterize adults (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Brown-breasted Kingfisher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Brown-breasted Kingfisher is broadly associated with forests, rivers and streams, and cultivated land.

A black cap and white neck collar separate the blue-backed, warm-bellied kingfisher from other regional species (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-capped Kingfisher is recorded from Mindanao (Lepage, 2026). Takes fish, lizards, frogs and large insects in coastal and inland wetland habitats (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The enormous red bill, sandy-brown head, warm yellow-orange underside and blue back distinguish this large kingfisher (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Stork-billed Kingfisher has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Pasonanca area, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Stork-billed Kingfisher is associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, and coastal and intertidal habitats. The Stork-billed Kingfisher usually hunts from waterside perches, diving for fish and crustaceans and also taking reptiles, amphibians and insects (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Blue-green upperparts and a white collar and underside distinguish the collared kingfisher (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Collared Kingfisher is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Collared Kingfisher inhabits mangroves, coconut groves and other coastal vegetation, with forest habitats also noted in the regional checklist. It hunts from exposed perches and takes crustaceans, fish, insects and other small animals (McGregor, 1909–1910; Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 43.4 mm, wing length of 91.3 mm, tail length of 60.5 mm, and body mass of 53 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 10.5 mm, bill depth of 10.1 mm, and tarsus length of 12.9 mm for Todiramphus sanctus (Tobias et al., 2022). The Sacred Kingfisher has been reported from Mindanao as an occasional visitor (Lepage, 2026). The Sacred Kingfisher is broadly associated with forests, rivers and streams, shrubland, and coastal and intertidal habitats.

The male Rufous-lored Kingfisher has deep blue upperparts, chestnut lores and a narrow chestnut band on the hindneck. A pale blue line extends behind the eyes across the nape, while the lower back is bright silvery-blue and the underparts largely white. Females have a broader chestnut nuchal collar, darker upperparts and a variable fawn wash on the breast (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rufous-lored Kingfisher has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Rufous-lored Kingfisher is associated with forests, coastal and intertidal habitats, and cave and karst environments. Bourns and Worcester recorded beetles, grasshoppers, spiders and grubs in the diet, with birds sometimes descending to the ground to feed (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

The broad bright bill, blue-green head, and conspicuous pale blue wing panel identify the dollarbird (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Oriental Dollarbird is reported from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include the Zamboanga Peninsula and the Mount Kitanglad and Mount Hilong-Hilong areas. Historical records also document it on Samar and nearby islands (Lint & Stott, 1948; GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Dollarbird launches aerial pursuits of large insects from high, exposed branches (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Oriental Dollarbird is associated with forests.

r.full: Lint, K. C., & Stott, K., Jr. (1948). Notes on birds of the Philippines. The Auk, 65(1), 41–46. https://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/auk/v065n01/p0041-p0046.pdf

records.p: Chestnut crown and mantle, an eye mask, and blue lower back contrast with the green underparts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Rufous-crowned Bee-eater has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Northern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Rufous-crowned Bee-eater is associated with grasslands and other open areas, agricultural areas, and forests edges. McGregor described nesting burrows excavated into level sandy ground, with a descending tunnel leading to an enlarged chamber (McGregor, 1909–1910).

AVONET lists a culmen length of 37 mm, wing length of 108.2 mm, tail length of 106.7 mm, and body mass of 29.5 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 5.9 mm, bill depth of 6 mm, and tarsus length of 10.7 mm for Merops ornatus (Tobias et al., 2022). The Rainbow Bee-eater has been documented on Mindanao, including Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Rainbow Bee-eater is broadly associated with forests, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as cultivated land.

An orange throat, blue tail and paired tail streamers characterize adults (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Green upperparts, rufous throat, blue rump and elongated central tail feathers are distinctive (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Blue-tailed Bee-eater has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Blue-tailed Bee-eater is associated with grasslands and other open areas as well as agricultural areas. The Blue-tailed Bee-eater catches bees, dragonflies and other flying insects on aerial sorties, often beating captured prey against a perch (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Adults combine gray head and breast, rufous-buff belly, and a dark graduated tail edged in white (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Plaintive Cuckoo has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Plaintive Cuckoo is broadly associated with forests. The species is a brood parasite; an account from Singapore documents an Ashy Tailorbird as a host (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Adult Sunda Brush Cuckoos have a greyish head and brownish-grey upperparts contrasting with a warm rufous throat and underparts, together with a yellow eye-ring. Females can have a barred rufous form. Juveniles are more heavily barred above and below, so the yellowish eye-ring and pattern of barring are useful features (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Sunda Brush Cuckoo has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Sunda Brush Cuckoo is broadly associated with forests. An account from Singapore documents brood parasitism involving Malaysian Pied Fantails (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Smaller and more lightly streaked across head and back than Greater Coucal, with a long tail and warm chestnut wings (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Lesser Coucal has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mainit Hot Spring Protected Landscape, Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Matutum, Surigao del Sur, and Bukidnon. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Lesser Coucal is broadly associated with forests. Often suns itself on an exposed branch with its wings partly spread (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The buff-colored head and neck contrast with a black facial mask and chestnut wings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Black-faced Coucal has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Black-faced Coucal is broadly associated with forests.

Black plumage with a purple-green sheen contrasts with rich chestnut wings and a long tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). Within Greater Mindanao, the Greater Coucal is listed from Basilan. A separate mainland Mindanao report in aggregated occurrence data is not substantiated by the regional range given in the 2025 WBCP checklist (WBCP, 2025; GBIF.org, 2026). The Greater Coucal is broadly associated with forests.

Rich chestnut wings stand out from the otherwise glossy black-green body and long tail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Coucal has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). Historical observers found it in high grass and thick brush, with breeding reported during February and March (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Coucal is associated with forests.

A small bronze-green cuckoo with a pale forehead, barred whitish underside and red eye-ring in adult males; females have a yellow eye-ring (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Little Bronze Cuckoo has records from Mindanao and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Pasonanca area, Davao del Norte, and Davao Oriental (GBIF.org, 2026). The Little Bronze Cuckoo is associated with forests. The Little Bronze Cuckoo feeds on insects including caterpillars in tree crowns; the Golden-bellied Gerygone is a recorded brood host (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Males have iridescent violet-purple head and upperparts, barred white lower underparts and an orange-red bill; females have a rufous-bronze head and dark bars below (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Violet Cuckoo has records from Mindanao, Samar, Bohol, Siargao, and Basilan. On Mindanao, records include Busa Mountain Range, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Agusan del Norte, and Surigao del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). Usually keeps to the canopy; known brood hosts include Brown-throated Sunbird and Little Spiderhunter (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). Caterpillars were recorded in the food of one bird examined by Bourns and Worcester (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The crest, white nuchal collar, chestnut wings and long dark graduated tail characterize this cuckoo (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Chestnut-winged Cuckoo has been documented on Mindanao, including Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Chestnut-winged Cuckoo is broadly associated with forests as well as coastal and intertidal habitats in the working regional checklist. A brood parasite, recorded using laughingthrushes as hosts; it may accompany mixed-species bird flocks (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

White and buff underparts are crossed by broad dark bars, and the tail has a prominent black subterminal band (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Indian Cuckoo has records from Mindanao, Samar, and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Tagubud, and Misamis Oriental. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Indian Cuckoo is associated with forest and coastal environments in the regional working checklist. The male has a grey head and breast, brown upperparts and conspicuously barred belly and undertail (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The Oriental Cuckoo is a medium-sized cuckoo with grey upperparts and a pale, regularly barred underside in the common grey morph. Adults have a yellow orbital ring; some females are rufous and heavily barred. The broad, relatively widely spaced belly bars and extensive white across the underwing aid comparison with other cuckoos, but it can look essentially identical to Himalayan Cuckoo without vocal or biometric evidence (Lewthwaite, 2023). The Oriental Cuckoo has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, and Agusan del Sur. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Oriental Cuckoo is broadly associated with forests.

r.full: Lewthwaite, R. W. (2023). Oriental Cuckoo (Cuculus optatus). In The Avifauna of Hong Kong. Hong Kong Bird Watching Society. https://avifauna.hkbws.org.hk/species/0040/006000

records.p: A gray upper body and strongly barred pale underparts characterize the adult cuckoo (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Himalayan Cuckoo is recorded on Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Mount Matutum. On Leyte, records include Mount Lobi Range, Mount Nacolod, and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Himalayan Cuckoo is broadly associated with forests.

Male Asian Koels are glossy blue-black with a long tail, red irises and a pale greenish bill. Females are dark brown above and paler below, with conspicuous white or pale streaks and spots. Both sexes show the red eye, and males can be separated from similarly dark crows by the paler bill and longer-tailed shape (National Parks Board Singapore, 2023). The Asian Koel has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Pasonanca area on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Asian Koel is broadly associated with forest edge, shrubland, and cultivated land.

r.full: National Parks Board Singapore. (2023). Asian Koel (Eudynamys scolopaceus). Flora & Fauna Web. https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/fauna/6/7/6767

records.p: In Eaton’s comparison of Asian hawk-cuckoos, the adult Philippine Hawk-Cuckoo has a pale slate-grey head and upperparts, a small dark patch on the chin, and largely unmarked reddish-rufous underparts. A conspicuous pale patch on the tertials is present, whereas a white nape patch is absent in the adult. Immature birds can show dark spotting and streaking beneath, so the adult characters should not be applied to juveniles (Eaton, 2018). The Philippine Hawk-Cuckoo is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Mount Apo Natural Park, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and Agusan del Norte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Hawk-Cuckoo is broadly associated with forests.

BirdingASIA, 30, 68–73. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333745229_Identification_of_Hierococcyx_hawk_cuckoos_and_the_first_record_of_Northern_Hawk_Cuckoo_Hierococcyx_hyperythrus_for_continental_South-East_Asia

records.p: An adult has a grey head, brown upperparts, rufous breast patch and barred white belly; juveniles are browner and strongly streaked (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Large Hawk-Cuckoo has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Matutum and Davao del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Large Hawk-Cuckoo uses wooded edges, secondary growth and mangroves on passage and during the nonbreeding season (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Large Hawk-Cuckoo is associated with forests as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

The Channel-billed Cuckoo is a very large grey cuckoo, darker on the wings and back, with a massive pale, downcurved bill and a long, visibly barred tail. The bill, body size and long barred tail together distinguish adults from other cuckoos (Australian Museum, 2022). The Channel-billed Cuckoo is recorded from Mindanao, where it is listed as a rare visitor (Lepage, 2026). The Channel-billed Cuckoo is broadly associated with forests. AVONET lists a culmen length of 82.8 mm, wing length of 339.2 mm, tail length of 270 mm, and body mass of 684 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 26.7 mm, bill depth of 31.4 mm, and tarsus length of 45.4 mm for Scythrops novaehollandiae (Tobias et al., 2022).

Adult Square-tailed Drongo-Cuckoos are glossy blue-black, with a slim, slightly decurved bill and a square to shallowly forked tail. White barring on the vent and undertail-coverts separates them from similarly dark drongos. Juveniles often show numerous pale spots on the head, body and wing-coverts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Square-tailed Drongo-Cuckoo has records from Mindanao and Leyte. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary and Mount Hilong-Hilong. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Square-tailed Drongo-Cuckoo is broadly associated with forests, shrubland, and cultivated land.

A short, nearly squared tail and velvety blue-black plumage distinguish it from the longer-tailed glossy drongo-cuckoo (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Drongo-Cuckoo is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Philippine Drongo-Cuckoo has been recorded in forest and secondary growth on Basilan (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The Spotted Kestrel has dark brown upperparts and paler brown underparts, with a narrow dark moustachial mark and yellow cere, orbital ring and legs. Males are described with a grey tail bearing a dark near-terminal band; females have more extensive barring and spotting, including multiple dark tail bands (Mallon et al., 2011). The Spotted Kestrel has been documented on Mindanao, including South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Spotted Kestrel is broadly associated with grasslands and other open habitats, shrubland, cultivated land, and settlements and disturbed habitats. AVONET lists a culmen length of 23.2 mm, wing length of 224 mm, tail length of 138.2 mm, and body mass of 162 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 9.5 mm, bill depth of 11.6 mm, and tarsus length of 41.5 mm for Falco moluccensis (Tobias et al., 2022).

A dark facial moustache contrasts with the pale barred underside and blue-gray upper plumage (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Peregrine Falcon has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Pasonanca area, Mount Melibengoy, Mount Tagubud, Lake Holon, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Peregrine Falcon hunts birds in the air using fast pursuits and steep dives. Some populations nest on cliffs or tall buildings (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Adults show dark slate-black upperparts with rich chestnut-rufous underparts and a paler throat (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Oriental Hobby has been documented on Mindanao, including Mount Kitanglad Range, Agusan del Sur, and Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Hobby is broadly associated with forests, grasslands and other open habitats.

Adult males show a gray head, rufous upperparts spotted with black, and a distinct dark moustachial mark (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Common Kestrel has been documented on Mindanao and Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026). Common Kestrels search open ground from hovering flight or an elevated perch and take small mammals, lizards and insects (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Common Kestrel is associated with grasslands and other open areas, agricultural areas, as well as settlements and disturbed habitats.

The very small falcon has a dark upper body and face with sharply contrasting white underparts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Falconet has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Falconet is associated with forests as well as grasslands and other open areas. Early observers recorded repeated use of exposed tree perches and brief insect-hunting flights followed by returns to the same perch (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Adults have an olive-brown back, bluish-gray underparts, strong digging feet, and mostly bare skin around the eye (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Megapode is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Busa Mountain Range, Mount Melibengoy, South Cotabato, and Sarangani. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Philippine Megapode is broadly associated with forests, coastal and intertidal habitats. Incubation takes place in mounds of organic material that warm the buried eggs (McGregor, 1909–1910). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Vulnerable (VU).

Male plumage includes prominent red facial comb and wattles, pointed neck hackles, and curved elongated tail feathers (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Red Junglefowl is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Hamiguitan Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Red Junglefowl is associated with forests. A nest recorded near Mariveles, Bataan, on 26 February 1904 occupied a shallow hollow sheltered by bushes and grass; it contained four cream-buff eggs (McGregor, 1909–1910).

Males show slate-blue head and breast, a black-and-white throat pattern and chestnut belly; females are brown with finely barred underparts (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The King Quail is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Lituban–Quipit Watershed, Mount Mayo, and Bukidnon. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The King Quail is a secretive ground bird of grassland and scrub that eats seeds and small insects (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Adult Hooded Cranes have a slate-grey body, a white head and neck, a small exposed red patch on the forehead and black flight feathers, tail and legs. Juveniles have a tan rather than white head. The contrast between the white neck and dark body makes adult birds distinctive among cranes (International Crane Foundation, n.d.). The Hooded Crane has an exceptional documented occurrence on Siargao Island, where a small group was photographed in 2020. This record does not indicate a regular local wintering population (East Asian–Australasian Flyway Partnership, 2020). The Hooded Crane uses wetlands, grassland and cultivated open landscapes in its wider range. The isolated historical Siargao record does not demonstrate regular local habitat use. AVONET lists a culmen length of 105.3 mm, wing length of 494.8 mm, tail length of 166 mm, and body mass of 3729.9 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 9.9 mm, bill depth of 15.8 mm, and tarsus length of 211.2 mm for Grus monacha (Tobias et al., 2022).

r.full: International Crane Foundation. (n.d.). Hooded Crane (Grus monacha): Identification. https://savingcranes.org/species/hooded-crane/

records.p: The olive-brown back and wings contrast with a slate-gray throat and chest and brown undertail (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Plain Bush-hen has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape on Bohol (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The Plain Bush-hen is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands.

White face and underparts contrast with a dark slate-grey back; the yellow-green bill has a reddish base (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The White-breasted Waterhen has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021; Pitogo et al., 2024; Gamalo et al., 2023). The White-breasted Waterhen uses freshwater and mangrove wetlands, sometimes swimming between patches of cover (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Breeding males are mostly black and develop a high hornlike frontal shield; females are brown and patterned (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Watercock has records from Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Watercock usually remains concealed among dense wetland vegetation but sometimes feeds in the open (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A red frontal shield and bill with yellow tip, white flank streak, and white undertail are field marks (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Common Moorhen is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Common Moorhen is associated with freshwater wetlands. The Common Moorhen swims and walks over floating leaves and other freshwater vegetation while feeding (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). A clutch of four eggs was recorded on Samar on 25 August 1896; the eggs were pale with reddish-brown spotting (McGregor, 1909–1910).

The Buff-banded Rail has a grey eyebrow and cheeks, warm chestnut sides of the head and neck, a broad orange-buff band across the upper breast and conspicuous black-and-white barring on the flanks and belly. Juveniles have paler, less distinctly barred underparts and a less pronounced breast band (BirdLife Australia, n.d.). The Buff-banded Rail is recorded on Mindanao and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, Agusan del Sur, and South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Buff-banded Rail is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, grasslands and other open habitats, as well as coastal and intertidal habitats.

Adults of the Barred Rail have a dark face and black throat bordered by a conspicuous white cheek stripe, a broad chestnut band across the upper breast, and densely black-and-white-barred underparts. The upperparts are olive-brown and the iris is red. Juveniles were described with a broader olive-brown breast band and less contrasting chin and throat (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Barred Rail is recorded on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Samar Island Natural Park (GBIF.org, 2026). The Barred Rail is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands. Historical egg descriptions record clutches generally containing four eggs, or occasionally three, with brown and lilac spotting (McGregor, 1909–1910). AVONET lists a culmen length of 43.6 mm, wing length of 142.8 mm, tail length of 52.5 mm, and body mass of 280 g (Tobias et al., 2022). AVONET also reports a bill width of 4.4 mm, bill depth of 8.5 mm, and tarsus length of 52.2 mm for Hypotaenidia torquata (Tobias et al., 2022).

Has a red-tinted bill, chestnut crown and nape, grey chest and finely barred upperparts and lower underside (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Slaty-breasted Rail has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). Usually remains hidden in dense wetland vegetation, emerging only briefly at cover edges (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

The white eyebrow and lower facial line frame a dark eye patch; a grey crown, orange bill and yellow legs complete the pattern (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The White-browed Crake has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Surigao del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026). The White-browed Crake is associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, grasslands and other open areas, and agricultural areas. The White-browed Crake is most active at dawn and dusk, foraging along floating vegetation and muddy margins (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Blue-gray to slate-blue body plumage contrasts with the strong red frontal shield and bill (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Philippine Swamphen has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Lake Lanao, Agusan del Sur, and Sultan Kudarat (GBIF.org, 2026). The Philippine Swamphen is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands. The Integrated Taxonomic Information System recognizes Porphyrio pulverulentus as a species, with Porphyrio porphyrio pulverulentus among its historical names (ITIS, accessed 2026).

A chestnut head, throat and breast contrast with dark barred abdomen and plain brown upperwings (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Slaty-legged Crake has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Malindang Range, Pasonanca area, Busa Mountain Range, Agusan del Sur, and Davao del Sur. On Samar, records include Samar Island Natural Park. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Senarillos et al., 2021). The Slaty-legged Crake is broadly associated with forests, freshwater wetlands, rivers, streams and agricultural landscapes. Partly nocturnal; migration records include birds encountering building windows at night (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

Chestnut head and upper breast combine with bold black-and-white bars on the wings and underparts (McGregor, 1909–1910). The Red-legged Crake has been documented on Mindanao, including Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary (GBIF.org, 2026). The Red-legged Crake walks slowly through wet leaf litter and shallow waterside vegetation to pick food from the substrate (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Red-legged Crake is associated with freshwater wetlands, rivers and streams, and agricultural areas.

A deep reddish face and breast, dark olive-brown back and red legs distinguish adults from other small crakes (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Ruddy-breasted Crake is recorded on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Mount Melibengoy, Lake Holon, Davao Oriental, and South Cotabato. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; Pitogo et al., 2024). The Ruddy-breasted Crake is associated with freshwater wetlands. The Ruddy-breasted Crake forages mostly at dawn and dusk, venturing a short distance from emergent vegetation (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

A small grey-brown bird with bright yellow underparts and darker cheeks producing a hooded appearance (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Golden-bellied Gerygone has been documented on Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Mount Kitanglad Range, Cinchona Forest Reserve, Lake Lanao, Lanao del Sur, and Bukidnon. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte. On Bohol, records include Rajah Sikatuna Protected Landscape (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Golden-bellied Gerygone is broadly associated with forest edges, shrublands, agricultural landscapes. Frequently stays high among tree crowns and is often located first by voice; acts as a brood host for Little Bronze Cuckoo (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

An olive-brown reed warbler with a conspicuous pale eyebrow and buff-tinged flanks (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.). The Oriental Reed Warbler has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, and Bohol. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Lake Lanao, Surigao del Sur, and Agusan del Sur (GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Reed Warbler shelters and forages among reedbeds and dense wetland scrub (Bird Society of Singapore, n.d.).

In the museum-based account by Williamson, the upperparts are pale yellowish-olive, with fine streaking on the crown and mantle but an unstreaked rufous rump and upper tail-coverts. The tail feathers are relatively narrow and pointed. The description was based on a very small historical specimen series (Williamson, 1976). The Streaked Reed Warbler has a possible historical report from the Bislig area of southeastern Mindanao. The observation remains unconfirmed and does not establish regular regional occurrence (Greensmith, 1990, as reviewed by BirdLife International, 2001). The Speckled Reed Warbler is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14.9 mm, wing length of 65.5 mm, tail length of 55.8 mm, and body mass of 8.2 g (Tobias et al., 2022). Its listed Philippine DENR category is Critically Endangered (CR).

records.p: A relatively large reed warbler with a long, rounded tail, a long narrow bill, and a subdued supercilium behind the eye. Compared with Great Reed Warbler, it typically shows a shorter primary projection, with fewer primary tips visible beyond the tertials, although some geographic forms are difficult to separate (Naturalis Biodiversity Center, n.d.). The Clamorous Reed Warbler has records from Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Agusan Marsh Wildlife Sanctuary, Mount Hilong-Hilong, Davao del Sur, and Davao de Oro. On Leyte, records include Mount Nacolod and Southern Leyte (GBIF.org, 2026; GIZ, 2013). The Clamorous Reed Warbler forages among reeds and waterside scrub, taking beetles, spiders, other insects and occasionally small vertebrates (Naturalis Biodiversity Center, n.d.).

The Oriental Skylark is a small, streaked brown skylark with a modest crest and a relatively slim pointed bill. Compared with Eurasian Skylark it has a shorter tail and shorter primary projection, and the inner wing lacks the conspicuous white trailing edge of that species. These comparative characters can be subtle outside a clear flight view (Hong Kong Bird Watching Society, n.d.). The Oriental Skylark has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include Bukidnon (GBIF.org, 2026). The Oriental Skylark is broadly associated with freshwater wetlands, grasslands, other open habitats, shrubland and cultivated land. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14.8 mm, wing length of 86.4 mm, tail length of 52.2 mm, and body mass of 26.3 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: A small, short-billed bushlark with heavily dark-streaked grey-brown upperparts, a buff eyebrow, a rufous margin along the wing and a pale underside. The breast is commonly streaked and the overall colouring varies among regional forms. These are broad field marks of the species complex, not a uniquely diagnostic Philippine subspecies combination (State of Victoria, n.d.). The Singing Bush Lark has been documented on Mindanao, Leyte, Bohol, and Siargao. On Mindanao, records include South Cotabato (GBIF.org, 2026). The Singing Bush Lark is broadly associated with grasslands and other open habitats and shrubland. AVONET lists a culmen length of 14.4 mm, wing length of 72.6 mm, tail length of 48 mm, and body mass of 23 g (Tobias et al., 2022).

records.p: The White-breasted Woodswallow has a dark blue-grey head, neck, upperparts and wings, contrasting with a clean white breast, belly and underwings. Its bill is blue with a black tip. Juveniles are browner and more mottled, with a thin cream eyebrow and warmer-toned underparts (Australian Museum, 2022). The White-breasted Woodswallow has records from Mindanao, Samar, Leyte, Bohol, Dinagat, and Siargao, including Mount Kitanglad Range on Mindanao and Eastern Samar (GBIF.org, 2026). A historical breeding colony along the Baco River, Mindoro, placed nests among the upturned roots of fallen trees (McGregor, 1909–1910). The White-breasted Woodswallow is associated with forests.
